title: Manunggul Jar
creator: Ancient Palawan Potters
description: In the Tabon Caves of Palawan, the Manunggul Jar is an exceptionally well-known secondary burial jar. The Manunggul Jar is dated to the late Neolithic Period and features an extremely detailed lid that has two human figurines in a boat as they represent a person's journey to the afterlife. The soul's journey to the afterlife represents a person's beliefs regarding spirituality, burial customs, and the skill of early Filipinos as artists, which confirms the importance of the Manunggul Jar as one of the most significant archeological finds in the Philippines.
subject: Burial Practices; Ancient Pottery; Neolithic Philippines; Spiritual Beliefs; Archaeology

title: Laguna Copperplate Inscription
creator: Unknown Ancient Filipino Scribe
description: The Laguna Copperplate Inscription is thought to be the oldest known written record found in the Philippines, dating back to 900 CE. The Laguna Copperplate Inscription has been inscribed onto a flat piece of thin copper and discusses the means by which debts were forgiven in the early political setup as a result of the early organized societies that existed at this time. The Laguna Copperplate Inscription also contains evidence of literacy, trade and cultural links to our neighboring Asian countries. The Laguna Copperplate Inscription serves to establish that organized societies existed long before Spain established itself in the Philippines by showing that pre-hispanic Filipinos had created systems for communication that were quite complex.
subject: Ancient Writing Systems; Philippine History; Pre-colonial Society; Trade; Archaeology

title: Butuan Ivory Seal
creator: Butuan Craftsmen
description: The Butuan Ivory Seal, a small carving made of ivory found on the excavation site in Butuan, Agusan del Norte, is thought to be an early method of marking documents or goods during trade. This artifact demonstrates the strong involvement of the early Filipinos in trade throughout all of Southwest Asia and the outstanding capabilities for artistry and commerce among those living in the Butuan area.
subject: Trade and Commerce; Ivory Artifacts; Ancient Craftsmanship; Butuan Civilization

title: Balangay Boats
creator: Ancient Austronesian Boat Builders
description: Balangay Boats are old wood vessels found at Butuan that are recognized as using today's definitions as the earliest examples of marine vessels in the Philippines. These vessels were utilized by the early Filipinos of Austronesian descent as modes of transportatiom or trade to other islands and countries surrounding the Philippines. Each balangay boat was built entirely from nailed-together wooden planks — an engineering marvel — representing the long history of seafaring skills possessed by the early Filipino inhabitants of this region of the world.
subject: Maritime Culture; Boat Building; Austronesian Migration; Trade; Transportation

title: Golden Tara
creator: Ancient Agusan Goldsmiths
description: The Golden Tara is an ancient gold statue that was found in Agusan; it is thought to depict a Hindu-Buddhist deity from the period before the Spanish had colonized the Philippines. This artifact is made from high-purity gold, which is a testament to the cultural and religious influences of early trade between India and Southeast Asian societies. The design of this statue exhibits the skillful craftsmanship of goldsmiths in the Philippines long ago and offers evidence of the thriving spiritual and artistic heritages that existed prior to colonization.
subject: Gold Artifacts; Hindu-Buddhist Influence; Religion; Pre-colonial Philippines; Goldsmithing

title: Surigao Treasure
creator: Pre-colonial Filipino Goldsmiths
description: The Surigao Treasure consists of many ancient gold ornaments, jewelry items, belts and ceremony objects, which were all found in Surigao del Sur. These artifacts emanate from before the period of Spanish colonization and illustrate the affluence, skill of workmanship, and social standing of early Filipino communities. The sophistication of their ornamentation and the use of pure gold demonstrate that the ancient Filipinos possessed a high degree of sophistication in their goldworking techniques and were well connected to other regional trading networks and networks of cultural exchange within Southeast Asia.
subject: Gold Jewelry; Wealth and Status; Ancient Filipino Craftsmanship; Trade; Archaeology

title: Calatagan Pot
creator: Ancient Tagalog Potters
description: The Calatagan Pot, a clay burial jar found in Batangas. It has important inscriptions engraved on its exterior surface. The pot may be associated with pre-colonial Philippine burial practices and ancient Filipino writing systems. This represents the spiritual beliefs, languages and everyday life of the Tagalog people in the early Philippines during the time prior to colonialism.
subject: Burial Traditions; Ancient Scripts; Pottery; Pre-colonial Culture; Archaeology

title: Angono Petroglyphs
creator: Prehistoric Austronesian hunter-gatherers
description: The Angono Petroglyphs are the Philippines' oldest known rock carvings, dating back to the late Neolithic period. More than a hundred stylized human and animal figures have been carved into a rock face at this site, believed to represent early forms of communication, ritual practices, or symbols used for healing by prehistoric communities. This site provides invaluable evidence of the art and culture, spiritual belief system, and everyday life of early Filipinos, prior to the written record in the Philippines.

title: Kamhantik Limestone Tombs
creator: Ancient pre-colonial Filipino
description: The Kamhantik Limestone Tombs, in Mulanay, Quezon Province, are an archaeological site of great significance that includes limestone coffins (burials) cut directly from large blocks of stone, skeletal remains and accompanying burial artifacts. Based on the tombs, archaeologists believe this site represents a well-organized, pre-colonial society that possessed an advanced knowledge of stone carving techniques and burial practices. The presence of these tombs suggests that a successful social structure existed, further defining the complexity and diversity of culture among the ancient communities of southern Luzon.

title: Banton Cloth
creator: Early Visayan weavers
description: Banton Cloth, which is one of the earliest existing cloth pieces from the Southeast Asian region, was found within a wooden coffin located in the area known as Banton Island in the Philippines. This cloth is comprised of a number of different types of fiber and is decorated with intricate geometric designs that were made using techniques for dyeing and weaving that resulted in highly skilled workmanship by the early Filipinos and reveal their impressive artistry prior to the arrival of European colonial authorities. Additionally, the Banton Cloth is indicative of the early trade patterns among various cultural groups, provides evidence of how people identified themselves through different methods and ways, and demonstrates how textile-making traditions are an influence on the way in which the culture of weaving in the Philippines has developed over time.
subject: Textile Art; Weaving Traditions; Pre-colonial Philippines; Anthropology; Material Culture

title: Maranao Okir Wood Carvings
creator: Maranao artisans
description: Maranao Okir utilize form and creative expression to create unique decorative art pieces created by the people of the Maranao tribe, who live in the Lanao del Sur region of Mindanao. Maranao culture has a rich tradition of creating Okir, which has flowing designs made with intricate line work that often utilize geometric figures (shapes) with influences from both the natural world (flora and fauna) and mythical creatures. Okir is also applied to various pieces of furniture (houses), special event-related items (boats), musical instruments, and ceremonial artifacts. Okir has both indigenous and Muslim cultural roots, and represents the identity through one's creation of Okir, as well as demonstrates the social status, pride, and prestige of the individuals associated with the Maranao tribes.

title: Ifugao Bulul
creator: Ifugao ritual carvers and spiritual artisans
description: The Ifugao Bulul is a carved wooden statue representing the spirit guardians of rice, and the ancestors of the people of Ifugao in the Cordillera region of the Philippines. These statues were traditionally placed in granaries and fields, and were believed to protect rice crops, foster fertility, and provide an abundance of rice at harvest time. Each Bulul was ritually ceremonially blessed, signifying the deep spiritual connections among agriculture, ancestors, and daily life in Ifugao culture. The Bulul still represents powerful symbols of Indigenous belief systems in the Philippines today.

title: T’boli T’nalak
creator: T’boli women weavers
description: The sacred textile, T’nalak, is made by the T’boli people of South Cotabato, using traditional handweaving techniques. Skilled women (known as “dreamweavers”) create these textiles, believing that the spirit guardian Fu Dalu reveals their designs in dreams. Creating T’nalak is very detail-oriented and requires a lot of patience, as the weavers use abaca fibers dyed in the traditional manner. T’nalak is used to create cultural items for rituals and ceremonies that represent identity and spirituality.

title: Kulintang Ensemble
creator: Maranao, Maguindanao, and Tausug musicians
description: The Kulintang Ensemble consists of a number of horizontally aligned gongs, with varying-gongs used to provide rhythm; in addition, drums are played along with these in order to add additional sound/texture while performing as part of their celebration, ritual, wedding, etc. culturally, this type of music is very spiritual(in addition to being social) and continues to remain a key component of filipino indigenous music.

title: Spoliarium
creator: Juan Luna
description: The Spoliarium is a large-scale oil painting by Juan Luna created in 1884 while living in Rome. This particular work depicts the remains of gladiators that had recently died being pulled off of the arena floor, underscoring how brutal and incredibly oppressive oppression really is. While the painting has historical significance, it is also commonly viewed as a visual representation of the struggles faced by Filipinos during the Spanish Colonial Period. As such, it is considered by many people to be one of the top masterpieces of Philippine Art and a powerful symbol of the national identity/resistance.
subject: Painting; Fine Arts; Spanish Colonial Philippines; History; National Identity
